title: The Island of Songs and Hums
markdown:
Regent Grizelda’s bronze wings beat the Island Signal Station courtyard as if the air itself had filed a complaint. She landed on the flagstones, preened one magnificent feather, and announced that the terrestrial dispute would be settled at once, by her, finally, and with the dignity the Sky-Cliffs deserved.

Lord Grumblesnap arrived on the next breath, a wet slap of bog and a rumble that made the lighthouse glass shiver. Marsh gas puffed toward the Gryphon. Elara’s eyes watered. She was the novice envoy for the United Realms, uniform already smoothed three times since breakfast, and the treaty table was still empty of signatures.

“Terrestrial?” Lord Grumblesnap snorted. Her warts pulsed with a visible tide of indignation. She smelled of damp earth and simmering resentment. “You redirected the Whispering Falls with your aerial antics, you feathered fluffball. The bog is parched. The ancient willows weep for want of a drop. The little bog sprites shrivel like dried berries.”

“My claims are ancient and just,” Grizelda said, beak precise as a letter-opener. “The mountain peaks have always held primacy. Our ancestors drew from the highest springs. Their lives depend on the pure water of the Sky-Cliffs. You cannot expect us to surrender what is ours.”

The station was a small, windswept thing on a rocky outcrop, more watchful seabird than palace, built for signals and for keeping peace between monster realms that preferred shouting. Elara had been chosen because she was clever and eager, mind sharp as a new quill. She also detested being wrong in public. A frown, a sigh, a misplaced eyebrow from a delegate, and her knees went to overcooked noodles. She had practised greetings until her voice was hoarse. She had not practised this.

“Perhaps,” she said, a little too high, “we could discuss the water after we’ve signed the accord. It is a very important accord.”

“Sign?” Lord Grumblesnap’s voice ground like stones. “What good is signing if the ground under my bog is drying up thanks to this aerial arrogant?”

Elara wanted to sink through the floorboards into solid rock. The signing table held two empty chairs, a blotter, and a treaty that looked very sure of itself for a document nobody would touch. She fumbled her notes. Every phrase she had filed under Useful sounded like taking sides, or worse, like not knowing what to do. A misplaced eyebrow from Grizelda would have been enough to undo her; two delegates in full cry was almost generous.

Pipkin, the goblin clerk, attempted to become a potted fern. His ears, large enough to catch a cloud’s whisper or a distant dragon’s grumble, flattened against his head. Spectacles fogged. He polished them with the pocket lint he kept for emergencies that were usually only emergencies in his mind. “The weather report mentioned a twenty percent chance of spontaneous mushroom growth on the signing table,” he had squeaked that morning. “Or the ink will be too blue. Imagine, Elara. Sapphire forever.”

Now he muttered, “The water. Is it slippery? Like a wet greengage plum?”

Worry, in Pipkin, made peculiar observations pop out like mushrooms. Elara’s heart sank with a thud. The bee in her bonnet, the one that hated public error, began to sting.

The floorboards trembled. A shadow filled the doorway, not weather, height. Gorok the Stone Giant stood there, grey-eyed as river pebbles, carrying no weapon, only a small carved stone bird in one earth-coloured hand. Realms whispered that he could move mountains with a patient push. Today he simply looked solid. Elara’s first thought was that the day had found a larger problem. Pipkin’s fern rustled in terror.

Gorok did not roar. He rumbled, tectonic and calm. “The Falls have flowed longer than feuds. Their path is a song. A song can be changed. It must be sung with understanding, not shouts. A melody of balance.”

He set the stone bird on the polished table. It watched them with tiny carved eyes. The bickering stopped, not because anyone had won, but because the most imposing guest in the United Realms had spoken as if the water were older than pride.

Elara took a shaky breath. Gorok’s words settled like a weight that was somehow kind. The delegates’ frustrated faces went still. Pipkin peeked from the fern, polishing cloth forgotten, ears perked.

“He’s right,” Pipkin whispered. “A song. And the Gryphon… she likes singing, doesn’t she? She has a very loud, very proud… caw-caw-caw.”

Caw-caw-caw. Gryphons. Gorok’s song. Elara felt the bee pause, as if it had noticed a window. She could keep hiding behind the unsigned accord. That would be safe, and useless. Or she could risk a public idea that might be wrong in front of a Gryphon, a Bog Hag, and a giant who moved mountains for a hobby.

“Regent Grizelda,” she said, and met the bronze gaze. Her voice steadied by a degree she had not practised. “Gorok speaks of a song. Pipkin has noticed your vocalizations. They say you have a voice that carries for miles. When this treaty is signed, you might compose a new melody. One that remembers the ancient flow of the Whispering Falls and welcomes the present needs of the bogs. A song of agreement, not of argument.”

She turned to Lord Grumblesnap, tone shifting toward the damp earth the Hag had brought in on her hem. “The moisture of your bog is a treasure. Instead of a muddy grumble, you could offer a resonant hum. A hum that acknowledges the Gryphon’s old rights and suggests new channels that honour the earth. A burble, like water finding a path.”

The delegates blinked. Nobody had accused them. The unexpectedness, delivered without a scorecard, seemed to take the wind from both wings and warts. Grizelda ruffled. A faint dusk-colour showed under the bronze. Lord Grumblesnap’s pulse slowed from furious throb to thoughtful thrum.

“A song of the Falls,” the Gryphon said, a glint in the sharp eye. “My ancestors spoke of its beauty. It could tell of the Sky-Cliffs and the whispers they held.”

“And a hum that respects the old ways and the new,” said the Bog Hag, gruffness thinning. “A hum that says we are here, and we need life.”

Gorok nodded and took the stone bird back into his hand as if it were a jewel. The lantern light, which had shivered across the floorboards during the argument, settled warm and steady.

Grizelda tried a note, experimental and proud, that made the lighthouse glass hum in sympathy. Lord Grumblesnap answered with a low burble that sounded, if you were kind, like a bog deciding to be polite. The stone bird on the table seemed, for a moment, to listen.

They signed. Not with a bang or a marshy splutter, but with the quiet of people who had found a different noise to make. Pipkin held the ink pot in both hands, ears radar-straight, as if the twenty percent chance of mushrooms might still arrive out of spite. Grizelda promised her song. Lord Grumblesnap pledged her hum. Elara did not feel the bee. She had risked being wrong in a room full of important faces, and the room had not fallen in. The ink, she noticed, was a perfectly ordinary, treaty-worthy blue.

The Gryphon and the Bog Hag left with squawks and nods that were almost cordial, bronze feathers and marsh-scent going down the path in something like step. Pipkin’s ears still twitched, but his smile crinkled his goblin face.

“So,” he said, nearly a normal squeak, free of the rusty-hinge tremor. “No spontaneous mushroom growth. And the ink is perfectly, wonderfully blue.”

Elara laughed, bright as the station beacon cutting the last of the tension. “No mushrooms. A treaty. And a rather lovely song and hum.”

Outside, the sun dropped into orange and purple. The Island Signal Station kept its quiet watch between the realms, stone walls and a single proud light, a place too small for grand pronouncements and exactly the right size for a song and a hum. Elara smoothed her uniform once, from habit, and found there was no crease to invent. Down in the dark, far below the rock, water found the channels it had been arguing about all afternoon, and began, very softly, to practise.
characters: Elara (novice envoy), Pipkin (an anxious goblin clerk)
audience: children aged 11-12, fantastic story for confident middle-grade readers
